newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: S.Africa looks to Asia for more oil.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa looks to Asia for more oil.

text.p: South Africa aims to increase crude oil imports from Asia to diversify sources of supply and is seeking investors for its fifth refinery, Minerals and Energy Minister Penuell Maduna said on Thursday.
"We have raised the issue of importation of crude oil from Brunei," Maduna told Reuters in an interview shortly before leaving for Kuala Lumpur with President Nelson Mandela.

"We will raise similar questions with Malaysia when we meet this afternoon," he said before Mandela headed for the last stop on a four-nation tour of Southeast Asia also took him to the Philippines, Brunei and Singapore.
Maduna said he had started talks on crude supplies from Brunei, but declined to give any details.
"We are hopeful that Brunei will give us a sufficiently good deal for us to import their crude," he said.
"We are a net importer of oil and oil products and we have to make sure that we have the best of deals."
Maduna said it was in South Africa's interest to diversify.
Brunei halted supplies to formerly white-ruled South Africa when worldwide sanctions were imposed a decade ago at the height of the apartheid struggle.
Maduna said he hoped talks with Malaysia would also open possibilities for oil exports to South Africa, and attract investments in the country's next oil refinery project.

Malaysia became the fourth-largest investor in South Africa last year -- behind more traditional partners Britain, Germany and the United States -- when the state oil firm Petronas bought 30 percent of listed South African company, Engen Oil.
"The Malaysians, in particular, are now participating in our economy in quite a robust way," Maduna said, saying the stake in Engen Oil had cost 1.9 billion rand (US$427 million).
Asked about the new refinery's configuration and likely equity scheme, Maduna said: "It's too early to give any details."
South Africa has four refineries with total capacity of nearly 500,000 barrels per day (bpd). Maduna said the country's current consumption was 600,000 bpd.
About 60 percent of its crude supplies come from Iran, and the rest from the North Sea, Saudi Arabia and Egypt.

South Africa's heavy dependence on Iran goes back to the close links established between the Shah of Iran and the apartheid government after the United Nations imposed sanctions on South Africa in 1962.
But South Africa recently received one of Iraq's first crude oil cargoes of Basrah Light, when the U.N. allowed Iraq to sell a limited amount to pay for food and medicine.
